newsitem.title: USA: Democrats pledge swift action on education.
newsitem.headline: Democrats pledge swift action on education.

text.p: Congressional Democrats promised Wednesday to enact a $52 billion education plan, saying it would be fully paid in line with their new less expansive legislative philosophy.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle and his House counterpart Richard Gephardt told reporters the six-year plan fit in with the modest "Families First" agenda Democrats hope will help them to victory in the Nov. 5 elections.

Republicans, mirroring presidential candidate Bob Dole's attacks on President Clinton, have been hitting at what they call "The Radical Roster" of big-spending liberal Democrats who would take over as chairmen of key committees should the party return to power.

But Gephardt said the potential committee heads were on board with the Democrats' "practical and realistic" plans. "The people who would be committee chairs were in the middle of putting this agenda together and they are fully committed to this agenda," he said.

Gephardt contrasted the "Families First" plan with the "very grand" ideas sometimes proposed by Democrats in the past. Referring to the Republican sweep of the House and Senate two years ago, he said: "The election was a wakeup call to us ... we heard it."

The result, he said, was a Democratic agenda that sought to deal with "kitchen-table, everyday problems," unlike the "Contract with America" on which House Republicans fought a national campaign in 1994. The agenda lays out goals in education, child health care, retirement security and a balanced federal budget.

Daschle and Gephardt said the five-part education plan, already part of Clinton's election promises, would be the first order of business in a Democratic Congress and would be fully paid for under the balanced budget plan, partly by cuts in business tax breaks and savings on defence.
It included $1,500 tuition assistance for the first year of college with an additional $1,500 for the second year for students getting at least a "B" average and staying drug-free.

It also would allow up to $10,000 a year in tax deductions for tuition payments for four years of college, provide funds to upgrade technology in classrooms, subsidise interest on tax-exempt school construction bonds and support programmes to ensure all children can read by the end of the third grade.
